P1.evidence: The best opening in the batch and the only genuine four-part frame: 'It's just about understanding, Fredilito, where you are today, know, where you want to go, what's been holding you back. And, you know, if I feel like we can genuinely help you, we have so many different options.' All four beats are present. Agreement was sought, if thinly — 'Cool? Okay.' P1a scores partial rather than hit because he checked the pre-call homework properly ('did you manage to go through the link before the call, of Trevor walking through?' — 'Yeah, the seven videos, and the testimonials') but never read back Kim's notes or the application; the prospect twice referenced information he had given Kim that the rep evidently did not have. The opener was a variant rather than the scripted question: 'what was it that you originally saw from Trevor that stood out to you enough to book this call?'

P2.evidence: The worst baseline in the batch and the one with the highest stakes attached to it. One check of nine ran. Work was covered thoroughly and genuinely well — the longshore role, the six-year wait, the shift pattern, the physical demands and the vehicle vibration all emerged. Nothing else did. Age arrived only because the prospect mentioned his birthday. Height and weight were never asked. Health conditions were never asked. Injuries were never asked — and the prospect had opened the call by saying he had come straight from a chiropractor appointment and, ninety seconds later, that he had sprained his lower back at work a month ago on both sides in consecutive weeks. Neither disclosure produced a single follow-up question about severity, diagnosis, current status or clinical advice. Training week, results, diet, sleep and energy were all skipped, on a 58-year-old working rotating night shifts of up to ten hours, seven days a week. The picture the rep had when he prescribed loaded ballistic training was a job description and nothing else.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran — 'would you say that you're living to 100% of your full potential right now?' — and produced a good answer about aches, pains and new injuries. 'How do you want to enter your 60s?' produced 'I'm not going into my 60s. Like, I'm still young. I'm showing up these young bucks.' But the phase stopped at the surface, and this prospect had handed over more depth than anyone else in the batch without being asked: a wife living in the Philippines he is trying to bring to the United States, a VA loan he intends to use to buy them a home, and a pension plus free lifetime medical cover for both of them that depends on him staying physically able to work for ten more years. He volunteered all of it at 00:15:52. P3f and P3g were never run, so the wife, the home and the pension were never connected to the decision, and the reflect-back never happened. The single most powerful why in this batch was left on the floor.

P4.evidence: P4f ran well and in the right form — 'What is the rationale in getting help with a coach as opposed to doing it yourself? Because there's YouTube, there's ChatGPT, there's Google, the information is out there' — and the prospect answered it himself and convincingly: 'there's also a lot of noise... it's like hit and miss.' P4e landed too: 'There's no accountability and there's no feedback.' What did not happen is the history. The prospect had hired a personal trainer twice to pass the longshore agility test and described it as money well spent, and that only surfaced at 00:32:14 in response to a different question. It is the strongest proof point on the call that he pays for coaching and gets results from it, and the phase designed to elicit it never did.

P5.evidence: The want-or-need question ran and produced the clearest self-generated consequence statement in this batch: 'I need, I need, because like I said, I'm trying to preserve my health. Because if I don't do something about it now, man, it's only downhill from here. And that's the last thing I need is not being able to work.' That is the two-year question answered before it was asked, and it earns P5d a hit. But none of the other three moves ran, and the rep then explicitly closed the phase down rather than opening it up: 'I get a sense of seriousness from you... You know the consequences of what life is going to look like.' Same pattern as the Soneel Raj call — the rep assumes the prospect has run the frame internally and declines to run it. Here the material was exceptional and unexploited: a man whose ability to earn, house his wife and secure his medical cover depends on his back holding up.

P6.evidence: The strongest phase 6 in the batch. The alignment check ran before any price and returned an unqualified '10' — the only ten anywhere in these twelve files — and the rep pushed for more with 'why not a 12 out of 10?'. A clear yes existed well before the offer, so P6c is satisfied and the price landed on real conviction rather than on nothing. The all-in question was still never asked, which matters here because the thing that would have surfaced is the one the rep needed most: the existing $1,000-a-month credit-repair obligation, which he only learned about incidentally while taking the financial picture.

P11.evidence: A payment was agreed and structured on the record — first instalment $1,200, then monthly — but processing happened after the recording stopped, so P11a is partial. The prospect himself prompted for step 3: 'So you're going to send me the contract and all that stuff?' The rep said he would walk him through it and immediately removed the notetaker. Whether the Trevor onboarding call was booked, whether the agreement was signed on the call, and whether the welcome email and Skool instructions were given are all unobservable and are marked not applicable rather than miss.

objection_plays.detail: Permission was sought properly — 'you're open to me asking you a couple of financial questions just to see what we can structure for you specifically?' — and four elements of the financial picture ran: cash on hand (a little over $5,000, just after payday), disposable income after bills (around $2,000), credit cards (none) and credit standing (damaged, actively being repaired). Investments and crypto were never asked. The isolation move never ran at all — there was no 'finances aside, is there anything else keeping you from being 100% in' — which matters less than usual here because the prospect had already given a clean 10 out of 10. The failure is not in gathering the numbers but in using them: with $2,000 disposable and an existing $1,000-a-month obligation running for two more months, a $1,200 monthly plan puts him $200 under water immediately, and that arithmetic was available on the call and never performed.

Genuine and specific doubt about programme fit for his age: 'he's in his 40s? So how does he know what somebody in their 50s, 60s or 70s or beyond, how can he formulate?', immediately preceded by 'I've got to start going through some of the testimonials to see some of these guys.' The rep answered with assertion rather than evidence — 'Through experience. He's been doing this for 10 years. All age groups, of all demographics' and 'At the end of the day, we're all human' — and never showed or named a single older client despite the prospect having explicitly asked to see them. The BURNED BEFORE and certainty moves were not needed here; what was needed was proof, and none was offered.
No request for time. He moved to structure and payment without hesitation.
His wife was discussed as a reason to buy rather than as an approval gate, and she is overseas.
Timing favoured the sale — he framed it as urgent himself, 'if I don't do something about it now, it's only downhill from here.'

The clinical-fit gap, and the most serious instance of it in this batch. The prospect disclosed an acute occupational lumbar injury sustained a month earlier, bilateral, still under chiropractic management, with an appointment attended that same day. The playbook has no move for this: no question to ask, no requirement to establish clearance, no route to defer the sale pending clinical sign-off, and no script for declining. Left with nothing, the rep did what the absence of a play invites — he folded the injury into the pitch as a problem the programme solves. This is a script gap with a physical-harm pathway attached and should be closed before any coaching is done on this rep.

Competing financial obligation, distinct from ordinary affordability and not covered by objection C. The prospect is mid-way through a roughly $6,000 credit-repair programme, still paying $1,000 a month on it for two more months, specifically in order to qualify for a VA home loan for his wife. The money play as written treats disposable income as available; it has no move for a prospect whose disposable income is already committed to a goal he named as more important than this one. The overlap was disclosed and never engaged with.

notes: Phases 1 and 6 were run better here than anywhere else in the batch — a real four-part frame, and a clean 10 out of 10 before the price — which makes the rest harder to read, not easier. One baseline check ran out of nine, on a 58-year-old with a month-old bilateral lumbar sprain who mentioned a chiropractor appointment in his opening line. The consequence frame was declined again despite the prospect supplying it himself. And the strongest emotional material in these twelve files — a wife overseas, a VA home loan, a pension that requires ten more working years — was volunteered and never used. The coaching point for this rep is now unambiguous and unchanged across six calls: run phase 2, and run phase 5. The points for the business are separate and more urgent: the playbook needs a clinical stop condition, and the instalment structures need a disclosed finance charge.
